## What you'll learn

- How matched metagenomes let you compute **expression per gene copy**.
- How to tell whether a change in transcripts comes from **community turnover** or from **regulation**.

## From strains to whole communities

In a defined community, you know the genomes, so you can normalise within each strain (Part 3). In the open ocean, there are thousands of species, most without a genome. Instead, you can sequence **both DNA and RNA** from each sample, and map both to the same [gene catalog](../gene-catalogs/index.qmd). Then, for every gene or function:

$$
\text{expression per copy} = \frac{\text{transcripts per cell}}{\text{gene copies per cell}}
$$

The data come from [Salazar et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2019.10.014). You normalised the metagenomes in [Part D of the gene-catalog lesson](../gene-catalogs/04-downstream.qmd): divide inserts by gene length, then by the median of 10 single-copy marker genes, to get **copies per cell**. The metatranscriptomes are normalised the same way, giving **transcripts per cell**. The setup cell does both:

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())

samples <- read_csv("data/tara_samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
kos <- read_csv("data/tara_kos.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  add_row(KO = "K03704", Description = "cspA; cold shock protein")
marker_genes <- c("K06942", "K01889", "K01887", "K01875", "K01883",
                  "K01869", "K01873", "K01409", "K03106", "K03110")

# copies (metagenomes) or transcripts (metatranscriptomes) per cell, for 12 KOs, plus cspA
per_cell <- read_csv("data/tara_ko_sums.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  mutate(per_cell = inserts_per_bp / median(inserts_per_bp[KO %in% marker_genes])) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(sample, KO, per_cell) %>%
  bind_rows(read_csv("data/tara_cspa.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
              transmute(sample, KO = "K03704", per_cell = cspa_per_cell))

cat(n_distinct(per_cell$sample), "samples,", n_distinct(per_cell$KO), "KOs\n")
```

## Cold-shock protein: genes or expression?

Cold-shock proteins such as **cspA** (K03704) help bacteria cope with low temperatures. K03704 covers the whole family of cold-shock proteins, and many bacteria carry several of them, so even warm-water samples have more than one copy per cell. Colder samples carry more:

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
cspa_genes <- samples %>%
  inner_join(filter(per_cell, KO == "K03704"), by = c("sample_metag" = "sample")) %>%
  rename(genes_per_cell = per_cell)

ggplot(cspa_genes, aes(Temperature, genes_per_cell, colour = polar)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "cspA genes per cell (log scale)")

cor.test(cspa_genes$genes_per_cell, cspa_genes$Temperature, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

But **more genes** doesn't necessarily mean **more activity**. The increase in transcripts could come from two sources:

1. **Community turnover:** cold-water organisms carry more cspA genes.
2. **Regulation:** each cspA copy is expressed more in the cold.

### Exercise: expression per gene copy

Join the metatranscriptome values (`sample_metat`) to `cspa_genes`, compute expression per copy, and test whether it also correlates with temperature.

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| exercise: ex_expression
cspa_both <- cspa_genes %>%
  inner_join(filter(per_cell, KO == "K03704"), by = c("sample_metat" = "sample", "KO")) %>%
  rename(transcripts_per_cell = per_cell) %>%
  mutate(expression = ______)

ggplot(cspa_both, aes(Temperature, expression, colour = polar)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "cspA expression per gene copy (log scale)")

cor.test(cspa_both$expression, cspa_both$Temperature, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_expression"}
Expression per gene copy is `transcripts_per_cell / genes_per_cell`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_expression"}
```r
cspa_both <- cspa_genes %>%
  inner_join(filter(per_cell, KO == "K03704"), by = c("sample_metat" = "sample", "KO")) %>%
  rename(transcripts_per_cell = per_cell) %>%
  mutate(expression = transcripts_per_cell / genes_per_cell)

ggplot(cspa_both, aes(Temperature, expression, colour = polar)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "cspA expression per gene copy (log scale)")

cor.test(cspa_both$expression, cspa_both$Temperature, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```
Expression per gene copy also rises in the cold (ρ ≈ −0.76). **Both** processes contribute: cold communities have more cspA genes, and each copy is more highly expressed.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_expression
#| check: true
ok <- isTRUE(tryCatch(
  is.data.frame(cspa_both) && "expression" %in% names(cspa_both) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(cspa_both$expression,
                     cspa_both$transcripts_per_cell / cspa_both$genes_per_cell)),
  error = function(e) FALSE
))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct: expression per copy also increases in the cold.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: expression is transcripts_per_cell divided by genes_per_cell.")
}
```

## How much is turnover, how much is regulation?

On a log scale, the equation becomes a sum:

$$
\log(\text{transcripts}) = \log(\text{genes}) + \log(\text{expression})
$$

So the variation of transcripts across samples splits into the variation of genes, the variation of expression, and a term for how the two vary together (their covariance). Let's compute this for every KO in the data:

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
paired <- samples %>%
  select(sample_metag, sample_metat, Temperature) %>%
  inner_join(per_cell, by = c("sample_metag" = "sample")) %>%
  rename(genes = per_cell) %>%
  inner_join(per_cell, by = c("sample_metat" = "sample", "KO")) %>%
  rename(transcripts = per_cell) %>%
  filter(genes > 0, transcripts > 0) %>%
  mutate(expression = transcripts / genes)

variance <- paired %>%
  group_by(KO) %>%
  summarise(
    # covariance first: below, `genes` and `expression` are replaced by their variances
    covariance = 2 * cov(log2(genes), log2(expression)),
    genes = var(log2(genes)),
    expression = var(log2(expression))
  ) %>%
  left_join(kos, by = "KO") %>%
  mutate(label = paste(KO, sub(";.*", "", Description)))

variance %>%
  pivot_longer(c(genes, expression, covariance), names_to = "source", values_to = "variance") %>%
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = c("covariance", "expression", "genes"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(variance, reorder(label, variance), fill = source)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(genes = "#2f6f8f", expression = "#e8590c", covariance = "grey70")) +
  labs(x = "Variance of log2 transcripts per cell across samples", y = NULL, fill = "Part due to")
```

- **Housekeeping genes** (tRNA synthetases, RNA polymerase, signal recognition particle): nearly every cell has one copy, so genes per cell hardly vary (blue). The little variation their transcripts have comes from **expression** (orange).
- **cspA** varies far more than any of them. Most of that is regulation, but part is turnover: the cold-water community carries more copies of the gene.

### Exercise: how much of cspA's variation is regulation?

Use the `variance` table to compute, for each KO, the share of the variance of log transcripts that comes from expression. The variance of log transcripts is the sum of the three parts.

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| exercise: ex_share
shares <- variance %>%
  mutate(total = ______,
         expression_share = expression / total) %>%
  select(label, total, expression_share) %>%
  arrange(desc(total))
shares
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_share"}
The total is `genes + expression + covariance`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_share"}
```r
shares <- variance %>%
  mutate(total = genes + expression + covariance,
         expression_share = expression / total) %>%
  select(label, total, expression_share) %>%
  arrange(desc(total))
shares
```
For cspA, about three quarters of the variation comes from expression, and the rest from gene copies and their covariance with expression. Since the two parts are positively correlated (covariance > 0), turnover and regulation push in the same direction: where there are more cspA genes, each copy is also expressed more.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_share
#| check: true
truth <- variance$genes + variance$expression + variance$covariance
ok <- isTRUE(tryCatch({
  cspa <- shares %>% filter(grepl("^K03704", label))
  nrow(cspa) == 1 &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(sort(shares$total), sort(truth))) &&
    abs(cspa$expression_share - 0.76) < 0.02
}, error = function(e) FALSE))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct: about 76% of cspA's variation is regulation.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: total should be genes + expression + covariance.")
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
## A caveat about the marker genes
The 10 marker genes are also the yardstick for "per cell", so their gene copies are close to 1 by construction. That's fine for this lesson, but in a real analysis, use other genes to check your normalisation.
:::

Salazar et al. did this for whole processes across the ocean. They found that gene expression changes contribute relatively less in **polar** than in non-polar waters, and suggest that polar communities will respond to ocean warming mainly through changes in **which organisms are there**, rather than through gene regulation.

## Check yourself

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("A gene's transcripts per cell are 4 times higher in sample 1 than in sample 2. Its gene copies per cell are also 4 times higher. What happened?", [
  {text: "The gene is induced in sample 1", correct: false, why: "Expression per copy is transcripts ÷ genes, which is the same in both samples."},
  {text: "Community turnover: sample 1 has more organisms carrying the gene", correct: true, why: "Each copy is expressed the same; there are just more copies."},
  {text: "Nothing: the samples were sequenced to different depths", correct: false, why: "Per-cell values are already corrected for depth."}
])
```

## Going further

- **Scaling up:** [Part E of the gene-catalog lesson](../gene-catalogs/05-production.qmd) shows how to run the mapping steps for many samples on a cluster. Map the metatranscriptomes to the catalog exactly like the metagenomes.
- **Statistics:** for differential expression with metagenomes, a good approach is to model transcripts with gene copies as a covariate ([Zhang et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btab327)).
- **Defined communities, hands on:** a Codespace version of Part 1 is coming.

## Key points

- With matched metagenomes, **expression per copy = transcripts per cell ÷ genes per cell**.
- On a log scale, the variation of transcripts splits into **turnover** (genes) and **regulation** (expression).
- Housekeeping genes vary little; environmental response genes such as cspA vary through both.
